name: Classic swept analog pad/lead: two detuned oscillators into a state-variable (SEM-style) filter driven by a triangle 'fin' filter envelope that rises then falls, modest resonance, mono mode with 8-voice stereo unison, light compression and tape echo, and an optional second oscillator pair through a different filter type swept the same way
goal: Recreate the classic 70s/80s filter-sweep sound from scratch. Use a low register and two oscillators slightly detuned for a phasing movement. Put them through a state-variable (SEM/Oberheim-type) lowpass and give the filter envelope a triangle 'fin' shape: a slow attack up and a slow decay back down with low sustain, so each note sweeps open and closes again; set envelope intensity, then add a little resonance (not too much). Switch to mono mode with full stereo unison (all 8 voices) and some detune for size. Finish with light compression and tape echo (no chorus needed). Optional: route oscillators 3–4 to a second, different filter type with its own fin envelope and detune, then blend both layers. More specific than our generic pad swell skills: up-and-down fin envelope on the filter plus mono unison stack.

source.title: Why This Classic Filter Sweep Still Sounds So Good

prerequisites: Analog-style synth with a state-variable or multimode filter and filter envelope, or Web Audio: two detuned OscillatorNodes → BiquadFilter lowpass with frequency automated up then down (implementation note)

inputs.name: fin_decay
inputs.description: Filter envelope fall time (slow), low sustain

constraints: Original synthesis recipe; not affiliated with any vendor named in the source. Recreate in browser/Web Audio (Polyrhythm Studio) or any hybrid synth with comparable modules; no presets, banks or samples copied.
The video gives shapes, not numbers, except 8 unison voices. Set times and amounts by ear.
Vendor preset names from the video are not used. The SEM/Oberheim-type filter is a portable alias for a 12 dB state-variable lowpass.
Amp drive made little difference in the demo, so it is optional.

steps.action: Init a patch. Choose a state-variable (SEM-style) lowpass, and if the synth offers vintage amp/envelope models, use them. Play in a low register with two oscillators slightly detuned.
steps.expect: Slow phasing between the two oscillators

steps.action: Shape the filter envelope as a triangle 'fin': slow rise to the peak, slow fall back down, low sustain. Set envelope intensity so the cutoff travels a wide range.
steps.expect: Each note sweeps up and then back down

steps.action: Add a little resonance, just enough to make the sweep sing without whistling.
Switch to mono mode with full stereo unison (8 voices) and add unison detune.
Add light compression and a tape echo. Skip chorus, because unison already gives width.
steps.expect: Finished classic sweep with echo tail

steps.action: Optional: enable a second filter of a different type, send oscillators 3–4 to it, give it its own fin envelope and some detune, then blend both layers (pull back if it gets too dense).

verification: Holding a note shows the cutoff rising and then falling without retriggering.
Turning resonance up makes the sweep peak clearly audible; turning it down returns a smooth sweep.
Mono + 8-voice unison sounds wider than the dual-oscillator patch alone.
